# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is the main learning resource for the course *Statistics for Machine Learning*, taken by second-year Bioinformatics students. It accompanies eleven two-hour lectures, each followed by a two-hour practical.

The aim is that you understand not only *how* a machine-learning method works, but also *why* it works and which statistical assumptions it rests on. A method that you can only run is a method whose failures you cannot recognise.

## How the course is organised

| Day | Lecture | Practical |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | Why statistics? | One gene to thousands: an expression matrix |
| 2 | Experimental design and confounding | Data quality and batch structure |
| 3 | Principal component analysis | Finding structure in samples |
| 4 | Cluster analysis | Clustering genes and samples |
| 5 | Likelihood, information and AIC | Read counts and variant calls |
| 6 | Generalised linear models: logistic regression | Methylation and tumour status: odds ratios, tests and calibration |
| 7 | The bootstrap and cross-validation | Honest error estimates, grouped by patient |
| 8 | Evaluating classifiers, KNN and SVM | Classifying tumour samples |
| 9 | Regularisation, PCR and PLS | Prediction when genes outnumber samples |
| 10 | Trees, random forests and boosting | Forests and boosting on molecular data |
| 11 | Gene set enrichment analysis | Simulated gene sets: over-representation and GSEA by hand |

The linear algebra the course relies on is reviewed in two appendices: [Appendix B](b-linear-algebra.qmd) builds the geometric intuition with pictures (norms, projections, eigenvectors), and [Appendix C](c-linear-algebra-details.qmd) gives the definitions, proofs and algorithms. Read Appendix B before Day 3.

The practicals use data that look like bioinformatics data: expression matrices, read counts, variant calls. They contain no gene ontologies or pathway databases, because the object of study is the statistics. Most data sets are simulated, so that the correct answer is known and your analysis can be checked against it.

## Conventions

The margin carries four kinds of note:

- **DEF**: a definition.
- **KEY**: a central idea to remember.
- **↪**: a link to another day.
- **⚠**: a common pitfall.

All code in the book is in R. Python versions of the exercises may be added later.

The textbook for the course is *An Introduction to Statistical Learning*, second edition [@James2021], referred to as ISLR. Each chapter ends with a reading guide.

## Software

You need a recent version of R, RStudio and these packages:




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages(c(
  "ggplot2", "car", "emmeans", "boot", "MASS", "broom", "dplyr", "tidyr",
  "forcats", "stringr", "GGally", "igraph", "plotly", "ggfortify", "HSAUR3",
  "cluster", "pvclust", "factoextra", "class", "e1071", "glmnet", "pls",
  "glmmTMB", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "randomForest", "gbm"
))
```
:::
